title: Balance — Image Wiki
text:
Balance
  Why one frame feels steady on its feet and another feels like it is tipping over, even though nothing in a picture weighs anything.

  
    Termvisual balance
    Also calledcompositional balance, visual weight, symmetry and asymmetry
    Not the same asvisual hierarchy, symmetry, white balance
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensSymmetrical and asymmetricalBe honest about what this isCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Take an image where a large dark figure stands hard against the right edge and the whole left half is pale, empty wall. Most people looking at it report the same odd sensation: the picture is leaning. Something wants to slide off the right side.
Nothing in that picture weighs anything. It is a flat array of pixels, and gravity has no opinion about it. But your visual system runs a weighing metaphor anyway, and it runs it whether you ask or not. That is visual balance.
The useful definition is negative: a composition is balanced when no single area pulls so hard that you stop seeing the others (SRC-032, SRC-033). Balance is not about elements being centred or evenly spread. It is about the pull being distributed.
Why it happens
Balance is downstream of Visual hierarchy. Every region of an image exerts some pull on the eye — its visual weight — and your eye keeps a rough running tally of where the pull is concentrated. When the tally sits far off to one side with nothing answering it, you get the tipping feeling.
Designers borrow the seesaw for this, and the borrowing is honest as long as you remember what is being swapped: physical weight is replaced by how much the thing attracts the eye, and distance from the fulcrum still counts (SRC-032). A heavy element close to the centre pulls the composition less than the same element out at the edge. That is why the dark figure jammed against the right edge feels worse than the same figure a hand's width further in.
What makes something visually heavy:



Heavier
Lighter
Notes




Large
Small
Real, but the weakest of these on its own


Dark
Light
On a light ground; it inverts on a dark one


Saturated, warm
Desaturated, cool
Warm hues read as advancing


Detailed, textured
Smooth, plain
Texture implies mass


Isolated in empty space
Packed among neighbours
Space around a thing loads it up


A face, a body, an animal
An object
Recognition beats almost everything


High in the frame
Low in the frame
Reported consistently; treat as convention


Known to be heavy (a house)
Known to be light (a shoe)
Your knowledge leaks into the picture



The first six of those you can verify on any image in ten seconds. The last two come from design writing that states them as established (SRC-030) without showing the experiments, so hold them more loosely than the rest.
Symmetrical and asymmetrical


Symmetrical: Perugino, Christ Giving the Keys of the Kingdom to St. Peter, 1481–83
Asymmetrical: Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, 1871


Perugino, Christ Giving the Keys of the Kingdom to St. Peter, Sistine Chapel, 1481–83. James McNeill Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, 1871 (Musée d'Orsay). Both public domain.
Perugino mirrors the whole field about a vertical line: domed temple on the axis, a triumphal arch at the same height and the same distance out on each side, small knots of figures echoing each other left and right in the middle distance, even a pair of slim trees. Fold the architecture down the middle and the halves land on top of each other.
That mirror has a consequence worth knowing. Whatever sits on the axis is now the only thing in the picture with no twin, so it becomes enormously important by default — here the temple doorway, and below it the key changing hands between Christ and the kneeling Peter.
Whistler balances things that do not match. The heavy mass is the black dress on the right; nothing on the left resembles it, and it is answered instead by the dark patterned curtain running down the left edge, plus the small framed print high up. Between the two dark edges sits a large plain grey wall carrying almost no weight at all. Cover the curtain with your thumb and the whole picture slides right.


Symmetrical balance puts comparable weight on both sides of a central axis. It reads as formal, calm, permanent, deliberate — and by construction it is half predictable, so it can go inert (SRC-032). Wes Anderson builds nearly every frame this way. Kubrick's one-point corridors in The Shining and the barracks in Full Metal Jacket use symmetry to feel institutional and slightly threatening. Bergman's Winter Light uses it to make a church feel stiff (SRC-098).
Asymmetrical balance puts unequal things on the two sides and lets them cancel out anyway. It is livelier and it carries more information per square centimetre, and it is genuinely harder to get right, because you are balancing four or five properties against each other instead of copying one half onto the other.
Two more cases you will meet. Mosaic balance is balanced chaos: a Jackson Pollock, a newspaper front page, a wall of graffiti. No focal point, uniform emphasis, and it works as an even field rather than as an arrangement (SRC-032). Radial balance arranges everything around a common centre.



Garbhadhātu (Taizōkai) Mandala, Womb World, Japan, Heian period, late 9th century, colours on silk. Public domain.
Radial balance in its purest form. There are several hundred figures here and the weight is spread almost perfectly evenly — yet your eye does not wander, it drops straight to the small seated Buddha at the middle of the eight-petalled lotus.
It is barely larger than the figures around it and carries no stronger colour. It wins mostly because every ring in the picture is concentric with it, so the whole structure points inward. This is the one balance scheme that hands you a focal point for free, which is also why it is used for sacred images and clock faces and almost nothing else — you cannot put the emphasis anywhere but the middle.


Be honest about what this is
Balance is a perceptual convention, not a physical law. Nothing falls over. What is real is that most viewers, most of the time, report the same discomfort in front of the same unbalanced frame, and that discomfort changes how long they look and what they take away. That is a strong effect and a poor law.
Which means deliberate imbalance is a working tool, not an error. Film uses it constantly:

The Dutch angle — tilting the camera so the horizon is off-level — exists purely to make the viewer uneasy. Fincher tilts hard in Se7en when Doe holds the gun on Mills (SRC-098).
Pinning a character against the frame edge with a wall of empty space behind them makes them look cornered.
Loading the whole frame into one corner and leaving the rest dead makes the subject look small, abandoned, or about to be swallowed.




Edgar Degas, In a Café (L'Absinthe), 1875–76 (Musée d'Orsay). Public domain.
Deliberate imbalance, done by a painter who could balance a frame in his sleep. Both people are shoved into the upper right; the entire lower left is empty marble table top, a pale wedge with a newspaper spar cutting across the corner. Squint and the mass is one lump in one quadrant.
Two things stop it recovering. The pair sit at separate tables, so nothing joins them across the frame; and neither looks at anything inside the picture — her gaze drops out of the bottom edge, his goes off to the right, past the border. There is nothing on the empty side to answer the weight and no line of sight to tie the halves together.
The result is the tipping feeling described at the top of this article, and it is the subject: two people sitting side by side with nothing between them.


The question to ask about an unbalanced image is never "is it balanced" but "does the discomfort belong here?"
Common mistakes

"Balanced means symmetrical." Symmetry is one way to get balance, and often the dullest. Most good photographs are asymmetric and balanced.
"Balanced means the two halves have the same amount of stuff." Weight, not count. One small red thing can hold down half a frame of grey.
"Empty space unbalances an image." Empty space is part of what you are balancing, and it can carry real weight when it has shape. See Negative space.
"An unbalanced image is a bad image." It is a tense image. Whether that is bad depends entirely on whether tension was wanted.
"I can measure it." There is no instrument and no formula. Everyone teaching this says the same thing: you judge it by eye, and the squint test is the only tool (SRC-030, SRC-032).


Testing balance in ten seconds

Squint until the image is three or four grey blobs. Where is the mass?
Draw an imaginary vertical line down the middle. Does one side dominate so much that you stop looking at the other?
Do the same with a horizontal line. Top-heavy and bottom-heavy are real and less often noticed.
If it is unbalanced, ask what the imbalance is doing. Tension, or an accident?
Cover the heaviest element with your thumb. If the picture suddenly feels calm, that element is what is loading the frame.
